yes_case.case: The closest past episodes are the GST Council's decisions to impose 18% GST on corporate guarantees between related parties (52nd meeting) and the clarification of GST applicability on Director's remuneration. In both prior episodes, the Council moved decisively to plug revenue leakage where financial or corporate structuring created grey areas in B2B transactions. The current episode regarding NBFC-to-bank co-lending services differs because it directly impacts priority sector lending and institutional credit intermediation, making the systemic push for tax uniformity collide with banking cost structures. However, just as the corporate guarantee levy overcame industry resistance due to the imperative of tax clarity and revenue enhancement, the fiscal logic of closing the exemption gap on financial intermediary services drives toward the exact same formal Council approval.
key_evidence: Past GST Council rulings on corporate guarantees and intermediary financial services
Persistent revenue maximization mandates driving indirect tax policy on financial services
yes_case.strength_reason: The analogy to past financial service tax clarifications is strong on revenue motives, though the specific impact on bank-NBFC co-lending introduces unique credit-flow friction not present in intra-group corporate guarantees.
yes_case.deliberately_ignored: Voting member alignments, state-wise political negotiations, procedural timelines of upcoming GST Council meetings, and the precise economic elasticity of co-lending rates.

no_case.case: The closest past fiscal episodes are the 2019-2020 GST Council deliberations on priority sector lending certificates (PSLCs) and the 2021-2022 disputes regarding corporate guarantee taxation between holding companies and subsidiaries. In both of those historical episodes, the Council faced acute revenue-protection pressures and initial industry-wide confusion over intermediation services. However, this current prospective action regarding NBFC-to-bank co-lending services differs fundamentally in its structural complexity and the severe systemic feedback loops it threatens. Unlike the PSLC rulings—which were relatively narrow instruments with isolated secondary markets—taxing co-lending services directly penalizes the financial inclusion architecture mandated by the central bank. Furthermore, unlike the corporate guarantee disputes which were ultimately resolved through retrospective clarifications, applying an 18% levy to foundational NBFC-bank partnerships risks structurally breaking capital flow into priority sectors before any consensus can be reached. The absence of preliminary consensus reporting and the unique multi-layered credit risk-sharing mechanics make this episode structurally distinct from past service-tax expansions, halting the Council's appetite for rapid formal approval.

The 2021-2022 GST Council deliberations on corporate guarantees between group companies

yes_case.case: The structural friction in the Indian indirect taxation system regarding the GST Council is governed by a defined constitutional mechanism (Article 279A) requiring a three-fourths majority vote, where the Centre holds one-third weight and the states collectively hold two-thirds. Historically, structural friction in the form of state-level dissent or bureaucratic inertia is routinely bypassed or negotiated through the Fitment Committee and Group of Ministers (GoM) consensus-building frameworks. When revenue leakage or regulatory arbitrage—such as untaxed financial intermediary services in co-lending—is identified by administrative machinery, the structural friction of inter-governmental disagreement rarely prevents formal Council approval once the fiscal imperative is established. The institutional machinery of the Council possesses high throughput for tax clarification circulars and rate rationalizations, meaning procedural friction almost never permanently blocks fiscal closure once tabled.
key_evidence: Article 279A of the Constitution of India establishes a predictable voting threshold of three-fourths majority for the GST Council.
The institutional pipeline of the GST Council utilizes Fitment Committees and GoMs to process and smooth over state-level structural friction before final votes.

Historical precedent shows that tax clarifications and rate adjustments on financial and intermediary services pass through the Council's structured deliberation phases without permanent institutional gridlock.
